title: Geo failover on-call playbook (draft)
summary: Working playbook for on-call SREs to execute controlled geo-level failover when an entire region is degraded or unreachable. Includes detection heuristics, manual DNS/traffic-shift steps, validation checks, rollback guidance, and a lightweight post-incident checklist. This is a draft — expect gaps around automation triggers and RBAC guidance.
content:
Purpose and scope:
• This doc is for region-wide failures (partial/complete) where a single AWS/GCP region serving inference or the control plane is failing health checks or experiencing >X% 5xxs and cannot be recovered within expected MTTR.
• Not for single-AZ or single-host incidents; follow local runbooks first.

TL;DR play: detect via multi-signal, shift traffic away from affected region to warm-standby region(s) using DNS/traffic manager, validate at edge and app level, then scale capacity in the target region. Communicate early.

Detection signals (combine; avoid flapping):
1) Cross-region latency/5xx spike: 3x baseline 95th percentile for 10m + region-specific 5xx rate >2%.
2) External health checks failing (edge/LDN/POPs showing degraded probes).
3) Internal topology signals: control-plane heartbeats missing from region control-plane leader for >= 60s.
4) Provider incidents (AWS/EKS node unreachable, GCP zone-wide networking) + route53/elb abnormal metrics.

Pre-checks before action (on-call should confirm):
• Confirm incident page and notes in SRE incident channel (Slack #sre-oncall).
• Identify affected services and dependencies (model serving endpoints, console, telemetry).
• Check warm-standby target region capacity (reserved pools, Dedicated capacity allocations). Use dashboard: Console -> Dedicated -> Region capacity view.
• Verify that target region has compatible model versions and quantization artifacts (models pinned by version). If not, prepare to promote or fallback to compatible variant.

Manual traffic-shift steps (DNS-first controlled approach):
NOTE: We prefer DNS weighted shifts with low TTL during controlled failovers. Use provider's API (Route53 / Cloud DNS / Cloudflare) where possible to script changes.
1) Put incident banner and short update in #sre-oncall and incident doc.
2) Set global edge health check to mark affected region unhealthy (if supported) to trigger automated failover in LB.
3) Update DNS weights: reduce affected-region weight to 0, increase warm-standby weights proportionally. Example Route53 CLI (replace ids):
   aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{"Name":"api.redwood.ai","Type":"A","SetIdentifier":"us-west-2","Weight":0,"TTL":60,"ResourceRecords":[]}}]}'
   aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{"Name":"api.redwood.ai","Type":"A","SetIdentifier":"eu-west-1","Weight":100,"TTL":60,"ResourceRecords":[{"Value":"18.1.2.3"}]}}]}'
4) For Cloudflare Load Balancer: set pool for affected region to 'disabled' and route to fallback pools.
5) If using anycast/BGP provider, coordinate with network on-call — prep BGP route withdrawals only as last resort.

Validation checklist (post-shift):
• Confirm DNS change propagated (dig +trace, curl --resolve). Expect partial client caches for up to 2x TTL.
• Monitor streaming logs for 5xxs/latency in target region for 15m.
• Run synthetic requests for critical endpoints (token-creation, inference stream handshake, embeddings) from multiple public locations.
• Validate model output consistency for smoke prompts (short eval set).
• Confirm auth/keys/KMS access in target region (particularly for Private deployments).

Scaling and capacity notes:
• If warm-standby has reserved GPUs: immediately increase autoscaling min to match expected QPS (see capacity playbook).
• If scale-up is needed in Dedicated pools, alert capacity-ops / sales-eng (they own reservation changes).
• Temporary quantization fallback: if large models exceed memory, switch to a smaller quantized variant — ensure team approval and log change.

Rollback guidance:
• If target region shows instability or degraded quality, revert DNS weights back to previous values slowly (50% then 100%) and/or re-enable affected-region pool if partial recovery is detected.
• Keep TTL high on rollback steps to avoid client oscillation.
• Record exact timestamps and API calls for audit.

Automatable tasks to prioritize (TODOs):
• Build a single CLI: redwood failover --from us-west-2 --to eu-west-1 --mode dns|lb --dry-run.
• Add a runbook play that checks model artifact parity automatically before shift.
• Add RBAC-restricted run for DNS changes with audit log export to S3.

Communication templates (short):
Slack incident update (first message):
"SRE: Detected region-level degradation in us-west-2 impacting text-gen. Initiating controlled geo failover to eu-west-1. Users may see ~TTL propagation window of 1-2 mins. Will post validation results in 10m. — @oncall"

Post-incident summary template (to paste into incident doc):
• Impact: N minutes of increased errors for customers in region X.
• Root cause: suspected provider networking flap OR control-plane leader loss (TBD).
• Mitigation: DNS weighted failover to standby region + capacity scale.

Runbook draft: health-check endpoints to flip (internal):
• /_healthz/edge -> mark unhealthy for region
• /_healthz/serving -> check model cache readiness

Edge cases and gotchas: 
• DNS TTL abuse: some clients ignore low TTLs. Plan for up to 5 minutes of residual traffic.
• Stateful sessions: if application uses sticky sessions, migrating traffic may cause session loss; send user-facing messaging if needed.
• Private deployments: customers with VPC peering across regions may have different routing implications; coordinate with account team.
• Monitoring blind spots: ensure telemetry collectors are not region-bound; otherwise, run ad-hoc synthetic from remote regions.

On-call decision tree (quick):
1) Is outage isolated to single host or AZ? -> local runbook.
2) Is outage impacting >30% of region's requests for >=10m AND there is no quick recovery? -> proceed to geo failover.
3) Is warm-standby capacity ready? -> if yes, proceed; if no, escalate to capacity-ops and consider partial traffic drain with HPA adjustments.

Post-incident action items (initial):
• Run full postmortem (owner: oncall) within 48h.
• Automate the CLI path for DNS shift (owner: infra team).
• Add region-level synthetic checks to early-warning dashboard (owner: observability).
• Confirm SLA/customer-impact list and notify CS for affected accounts (owner: incident commander).

Loose notes / open questions (bring to SRE weekly):
• Should we prefer LB-level failover over DNS for lower propagation in large customers? pros/cons.
• Minimum warm-standby capacity per customer tier? current policy unclear.
• Add a canary stage: shift 10% first for 5m then 100% if stable — how to automate safely?

References and past incidents:
• SRE incident SRE-9812 (2025-11): EU->US failover during provider maintenance — lessons: always verify KMS in target region.
• Confluence playbook (link id CONFLUENCE-4567) for DNS procedures.

End of draft. This doc is intentionally terse in places to serve as an on-call cheat sheet. Expect follow-ups to expand automation, exact CLI commands, and RBAC workflow.
